title: Chicken leg, drumstick and thigh, baked, coated, skin/coating eaten

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken legs, drumsticks and thighs are dark meat cuts rich in protein and healthy fats. When baked with a coating (such as breading, sauce, or marinade) they develop a flavorful crust while the skin remains edible, adding extra taste and texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Dark meat contains more iron and zinc than white meat.
Baking with a coating creates a crispy crust through the Maillard reaction while keeping the meat juicy.
These cuts are staples in many cuisines, from American BBQ to Asian teriyaki dishes.
Chicken skin is a source of collagen, beneficial for skin, joints, and connective tissue.
If over‑cooked, the skin can become tough and bitter rather than crisp.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: A 100 g serving provides about 20–25 g of complete protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Contains healthy fats
items.content: The meat includes monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fatty acids that support heart health when eaten in moderation.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Rich in niacin (B3) and vitamin B6, which aid energy metabolism and nervous‑system function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Provides iron, zinc, and phosphorus, important for immunity, bone health, and metabolic processes.

items.title: Collagen from skin
items.content: Edible skin adds extra collagen, which may help maintain skin elasticity and joint health.

items.title: Calorie density
items.content: Baked, coated pieces with skin can be calorie‑rich; portion control is advisable, especially on weight‑loss diets.

items.title: Saturated fat content
items.content: Skin contains saturated fats; individuals with high cholesterol should consume it in moderation.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Chicken must reach an internal temperature of at least 74 °C to eliminate salmonella and other pathogens.

items.title: Chicken protein allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to chicken proteins.

items.title: Sodium in coatings
items.content: Prepared breadings and sauces often contain added salt; choose low‑sodium options if you have hypertension.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the baked legs, drumsticks or thighs as a main dish, slice them for salads, add to soups, or use in sandwiches. The skin and coating are eaten together with the meat, providing crunch and flavor. If preferred, the skin can be removed before serving.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep raw chicken refrigerated at +2–4 °C for up to 2 days. Cooked meat stores in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 3 days. For longer storage, freeze in a sealed bag at –18 °C for up to 4 months. Reheat thoroughly before consumption.
